notes:
I found sources for most of Romans 1, but coverage is uneven. Verses 1–8 and 16–32 are well covered. Verses 9–15 are thin: one short summary plus the Enduring Word text, which cut off at verse 8. I found nothing from bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes, oca.org (Orthodox), or the Lutheran and Pentecostal sites. I also found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. Those categories are left out.

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1** Guzik says Paul calls himself first a servant of Jesus Christ and only second an apostle. He quotes Morris that *doulos* means "complete and utter devotion, not the abjectness which was the normal condition of the slave." He also notes the gospel is "of God" because it belongs to God; Paul didn't invent it, he only carries it. Clarke and Poole, both quoted by Guzik, suggest "set apart" may play on "Pharisee," which means a separatist. Once separated to the law, Paul is now separated to the gospel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-1/

**v. 2** Guzik: the gospel is not new or made up by people. It is very old in God's plan, promised through the prophets. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-1/

**v. 3** Guzik: Jesus is the centre of Paul's gospel. His human origin is his birth from David's line; the proof of his deity is the resurrection. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-1/

**v. 4** *Traditional reading:*
- Guzik quotes Clarke: "declared" (*horizo*, the root of "horizon") means a display so clear it can't be doubted. He also quotes Morris that Jesus was the Son of God in weakness before the resurrection and in power afterwards. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-1/
- Ellicott: "with power" means "in a transcendent and superhuman manner," and "Spirit of holiness" is set against "according to the flesh," where we would expect "in His divine nature." — https://biblehub.com/romans/1-4.htm
- Calvin: the power that raised Christ was like a decree proclaiming him Son of God, as in Psalm 2:7, where the "begetting" means what was made known. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/1-4.html
- Barnes (Presbyterian) insists Jesus "was not constituted, but declared or evidenced to be, 'the Son of God with power by the resurrection'". — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/1-4.html

*Points of debate:*
- **Does "with power" go with "declared" or with "Son of God"?** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note that Luther, Beza, Bengel and Alford read "powerfully declared," while they prefer "Son of God in power." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/1-4.htm. Constable also prefers "powerful Son." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/1-4.html
- **"Declared" or "appointed"?** The Pulpit Commentary notes the verb points to the resurrection, not to Christ's existence before his birth. It cites Pearson's view that Christ was "constituted" Son of God with power at the resurrection. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/1-4.htm
- **A current Reformed debate.** A Gospel Coalition (Themelios) article reports that Gaffin and James Scott read the verse as Christ's "adoption" at the resurrection. The authors agree Jesus was "appointed" Son-of-God-in-power then. But they hold the change is "not in the divine nature or in the Son's relationship to the Father, but in Christ's role in redemptive history." — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/jesus-adopted-son-of-god/
- **"Spirit of holiness."** Gann's note lists two readings: the Holy Spirit, or Jesus' own spirit kept holy. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/1-4.html
- **An early creed?** The Light of Israel commentary notes several scholars think verses 3–4 sound like an early Christian creed that Paul is quoting. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/1-4.html

**v. 5** Guzik: the gospel changes lives; it isn't theory. Grace and apostleship were given partly to produce "obedience to the faith," and the gospel must go to all nations. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-1/

**v. 6** Guzik: the fact that the gospel reached Rome shows these believers are "the called of Jesus Christ." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-1/

**v. 7** Guzik quotes Spurgeon: the Romans did not become called because they were saints; they became saints through the calling. "Grace and peace" joins the Greek and Jewish greetings, and both are gifts from God, not just good wishes. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-1/

**v. 8** Guzik: Paul didn't found the Roman church, which seems to have begun on its own as Christians moved to the city. He adds that there is "no Biblical or historical evidence" Peter founded it. This is a Protestant claim; I found no Catholic reply to it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-1/

**vv. 9–15** All I found is a short summary in Bridgeway's commentary. Paul prays for the Romans and wants to visit so that both sides are strengthened by each other's spiritual gifts. His duty to preach to all nations and cultures makes him eager to come to Rome. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/1-17.html

**v. 16** Deffinbaugh: verses 16–17 give the positive reasons for Paul's boldness: people are saved and God's character is revealed. Verse 18 adds a further reason: all people are condemned, and the gospel is their only hope. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-present-wrath-god-romans-115-32

**v. 17** *Traditional / Reformation reading:*
- Guzik says "righteousness of God" here is not the standard that condemns us. It means God's verdict of righteousness that He gives to the believer through faith. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-1/
- R.C. Sproul (Reformed): Augustine noted this is not the righteousness by which God himself is righteous. It is the righteousness God provides to people who have none, which Luther called "alien righteousness." — https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/just-shall-live-faith
- John MacArthur's ministry (Baptist) calls it the truth "that God's righteousness could become the sinner's righteousness" through faith alone. — https://gty.org/library/Articles/A194
- The Gospel Coalition: "Justification isn't a process; it's a declaration by God of our righteousness in Christ, immediately imputed to us." — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/martin-luther-breakthrough/

*Other Protestant readings (all on one StudyLight page):* https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/1-17.html
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist).** "Righteousness of God" means God's way of saving sinners. "From faith to faith" means the faith of the old covenant leading on to the faith of the new. He thinks "the just by faith shall live" is probably the right reading.
- **Coffman (Restoration Movement / Churches of Christ).** Holds the phrase means God's own character, not a righteousness credited to people. He rejects reading "from faith to faith" as "faith alone," pointing to James 2:24.
- **Hodge (Reformed).** Coffman reports that Hodge read it as "by faith alone."

**v. 18** *Traditional reading:*
- bible.org's exposition: God's wrath is not an uncontrolled emotion but his settled hatred for sin, continually revealed in his giving people over to their sinful folly. — https://bible.org/book/export/html/2335
- Desiring God: "God reveals his wrath against sin by giving people up to be more sinful." — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-wrath-of-god-against-ungodliness-and-unrighteousness

*Points of debate:*
- **Present or future wrath?** Deffinbaugh says chapter 1 is about wrath God is showing now, and chapter 2 about wrath still to come. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-present-wrath-god-romans-115-32
- **Who is condemned?** Got Questions reads the passage as about "unrighteous Gentiles." — https://www.gotquestions.org/God-gave-them-over.html. Deffinbaugh rejects a Gentiles-only reading. He thinks verses 19–20 aim mainly at pagans and verse 32 more at Jews. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-present-wrath-god-romans-115-32

**v. 19** Pulpit Commentary: even without the Bible, God shows himself outwardly in nature and inwardly in conscience. — https://biblehub.com/romans/1-20.htm

**v. 20** *Traditional reading:*
- Ellicott: "Godhead" is better translated "divinity," meaning divine nature rather than personality. "Without excuse" means they couldn't plead ignorance. — https://biblehub.com/romans/1-20.htm
- Poole: God gives everyone enough knowledge to leave them without excuse. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/1-20.htm
- Barnes: people are held responsible only when they have the means to know. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/1-20.htm

*Points of debate – natural theology:*
- **Ligonier (Reformed).** Natural revelation is real but limited; it shows God's power and our duty to worship. — https://www.ligonier.org/learn/devotionals/natural-revelation
- **John MacArthur's ministry.** "God's self-revelation through His creation is not enough to save sinners—it's only enough to damn them." — https://www.gty.org/blogs/B180917/knowledge-that-condemns
- **The Gospel Coalition.** These verses have sometimes been used to support arguments for God's existence. The writer says Paul's wording suggests a knowledge of God that is "far more immediate, intuitive, and universally accessible." — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/the-existence-of-god/
- **Catholic.** Catholic Answers cites the First Vatican Council, which declared that God can be known with certainty by natural reason. It adds that many scholars think Paul draws on Wisdom 13:5. — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-case-for-natural-theology

**vv. 21–23** Deffinbaugh: seeing God in creation should lead people to honour and thank him; instead they swapped his glory for images. Humans were made to reflect God's image, so bowing to creatures turns the created order upside down. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-present-wrath-god-romans-115-32

**v. 24** *What does "God gave them over" mean?* Most views are on one StudyLight page: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/1-24.html
- **Calvin (Reformed).** God does more than permit. By just judgment he arranges things so people are carried into madness by their own lusts and by the devil.
- **Wesley (Methodist).** God gives them up "by withdrawing his restraining grace." Benson, also Methodist, says the same.
- **Barnes.** God simply stopped restraining them and did nothing positive to push them into sin.
- **Haydock (Catholic).** Following Chrysostom, God *permitted* them to fall into these sins as punishment.
- **Ellicott.** The first step is the person's free choice, and exactly how much is human sin and how much divine judgment can't be pinned down.

Further views:
- Alford and Hodge, quoted on Precept Austin: the giving over is "not merely permissive, but judicial." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_124-32
- bible.org's exposition: the giving over need not be permanent and can serve to heal; God lets people taste the ruin of sin so they cry out to Him. — https://bible.org/book/export/html/2335

**v. 25** Deffinbaugh: people refused to honour God, so God lets them dishonour themselves. How they treat God becomes the measure of how God lets them treat themselves. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-present-wrath-god-romans-115-32

**vv. 26–27**
- *Traditional reading:* the Bible Hub study notes say "natural relations" means heterosexual relationships as God designed them and "unnatural" means homosexual behaviour. — https://biblehub.com/study/romans/1-26.htm. Constable notes the Greek words mean "females" and "males." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/1-27.html. Deffinbaugh treats "the due penalty" as God's judgment. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-present-wrath-god-romans-115-32
- *Modern revisionist reading:* Desiring God responds to the view that Paul condemns only heterosexual people acting against their own nature. It argues verse 27 makes that unlikely. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-other-dark-exchange-homosexuality. A commentary excerpt on StudyLight argues that Greek pederasty (men with boys) doesn't explain the passage, which describes adults on both sides. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/1-26.html

**v. 28** Matthew Henry, cited on StudyLight: a "reprobate mind" is one that can no longer tell things apart in spiritual matters. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/1-24.html. Deffinbaugh: rejecting the truth about God in the mind led to moral collapse. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-present-wrath-god-romans-115-32

**vv. 29–31** Got Questions: this is a choice that leads into a downward spiral, and removing the Spirit's restraint lets all wickedness follow. — https://www.gotquestions.org/God-gave-them-over.html. Deffinbaugh thinks the three "gave them over" sections are probably not a step-by-step sequence. He reads them as three examples of God's present wrath. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-present-wrath-god-romans-115-32

**v. 32** Calvin: they removed the line between good and evil and approved, in themselves and others, what they knew God condemns. — https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom38/calcom38.v.vii.html. A sermon on Bible Hub: enjoying other people's sins is a separate and greater sin, the furthest human corruption can go. — https://biblehub.com/sermons/romans/1-4.htm. Deffinbaugh: verse 32 leads into 2:1, where Paul moves from people who approve of sin to people who condemn it. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-present-wrath-god-romans-115-32
